     3	module MPY-SUBSCRIPT
     4	  imports MPY-CORE
     5	
     6	  // ==== positional access + negative-index normalization (used only here) ===
     7	  // valSeqAt is [total]: in-bounds vCons access reduces as usual; on an OPAQUE sequence (e.g.
     8	  // a trusted sort's sortVS(VS)) or OOB it stays an abstract total value — so indexing the
     9	  // opaque sorted list is DEFINED (no undischarged #Ceil), matching the old semantics' total
    10	  // atK. K trusts the [total] annotation; valid programs index in-bounds.
    11	  syntax Val ::= valSeqAt(ValSeq, Int) [function, total]
    12	  rule valSeqAt(vCons(V:Val, _:ValSeq), 0)     => V
    13	  rule valSeqAt(vCons(_:Val, S:ValSeq), I:Int) => valSeqAt(S, I -Int 1)
    14	       requires I >Int 0
    15	
    16	  syntax Int ::= intSeqAt(IntSeq, Int) [function]
    17	  rule intSeqAt(iCons(C:Int, _:IntSeq), 0)     => C
    18	  rule intSeqAt(iCons(_:Int, S:IntSeq), I:Int) => intSeqAt(S, I -Int 1)
    19	       requires I >Int 0
    20	
    21	  syntax Int ::= normIdx(Int, Int) [function, total]
    22	  rule normIdx(I:Int, LEN:Int) => I +Int LEN requires I  <Int 0
    23	  rule normIdx(I:Int, _:Int)   => I          requires I >=Int 0
    24	
    25	  // ==== Subscript: indexing obj[i] (list / tuple / str) =====================
    26	  // contexts (not strict attrs): the Index slot's Slice alternative must never heat
    27	  context Subscript(HOLE, _)
    28	  context Subscript(_:Val, HOLE:Expr)
    29	
    30	  // heap-object deref (covers both the index and slice forms via the Index slot)
    31	  rule <k> Subscript(ref(H:Int), IX:Index) => Subscript(V, IX) ... </k>
    32	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    33	       [priority(40)]
    34	
    35	  rule <k> Subscript(OBJ:Val, I:Int) => applyIndex(OBJ, I) ... </k>
    36	
    37	  syntax Val ::= applyIndex(Val, Int) [function]
    38	  rule applyIndex(list(VS:ValSeq),  I:Int) => valSeqAt(VS, normIdx(I, vsLen(VS)))
    39	  rule applyIndex(tuple(VS:ValSeq), I:Int) => valSeqAt(VS, normIdx(I, vsLen(VS)))
    40	  rule applyIndex(str(IS:IntSeq),   I:Int)
    41	    => str(iCons(intSeqAt(IS, normIdx(I, isLen(IS))), .IntSeq))
    42	
    43	  // ==== Slice: obj[lo:hi:step] (list / str) — CPython slice.indices ==========
    44	  syntax KItem ::= #evalB(Bound) | "#toSome"
    45	                 | #slLo(Val, Bound, Bound)
    46	                 | #slHi(Val, OptInt, Bound)
    47	                 | #slStep(Val, OptInt, OptInt)
    48	
    49	  syntax OptInt ::= "noB" | someB(Int)
    50	  rule <k> #evalB(NoBound)  => noB ... </k>
    51	  rule <k> #evalB(E:Expr)   => E ~> #toSome ... </k>
    52	  rule <k> I:Int ~> #toSome => someB(I) ... </k>
    53	
    54	  rule <k> Subscript(OBJ:Val, Slice(LO:Bound, HI:Bound, ST:Bound)) => #evalB(LO) ~> #slLo(OBJ, HI, ST) ... </k>
    55	  rule <k> LO:OptInt ~> #slLo(OBJ:Val, HI:Bound, ST:Bound)   => #evalB(HI) ~> #slHi(OBJ, LO, ST) ... </k>
    56	  rule <k> HI:OptInt ~> #slHi(OBJ:Val, LO:OptInt, ST:Bound)  => #evalB(ST) ~> #slStep(OBJ, LO, HI) ... </k>
    57	  // a list slice constructs a NEW object; a str slice stays a value
    58	  rule <k> ST:OptInt ~> #slStep(list(VS:ValSeq), LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt)
    59	        => #alloc(doSlice(list(VS), LO, HI, ST)) ... </k>
    60	       [priority(45)]
    61	  rule <k> ST:OptInt ~> #slStep(OBJ:Val, LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt) => doSlice(OBJ, LO, HI, ST) ... </k>
    62	
    63	  syntax Val ::= doSlice(Val, OptInt, OptInt, OptInt) [function]
    64	  rule doSlice(list(VS:ValSeq), LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt, ST:OptInt)
    65	    => list(buildVS(VS, slStart(LO, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStop(HI, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStep(ST)))
    66	  rule doSlice(tuple(VS:ValSeq), LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt, ST:OptInt)
    67	    => tuple(buildVS(VS, slStart(LO, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStop(HI, ST, vsLen(VS)), slStep(ST)))
    68	  rule doSlice(str(IS:IntSeq), LO:OptInt, HI:OptInt, ST:OptInt)
    69	    => str(buildIS(IS, slStart(LO, ST, isLen(IS)), slStop(HI, ST, isLen(IS)), slStep(ST)))
    70	
    71	  // ==== slice.indices: step / start / stop / clamp ==========================
    72	  syntax Int ::= slStep(OptInt) [function, total]
    73	  rule slStep(noB)          => 1
    74	  rule slStep(someB(S:Int)) => S
    75	
    76	  syntax Int ::= slStart(OptInt, OptInt, Int) [function]
    77	  rule slStart(noB,          ST:OptInt, _LEN:Int) => 0
    78	       requires slStep(ST) >Int 0
    79	  rule slStart(noB,          ST:OptInt, LEN:Int)  => LEN -Int 1
    80	       requires slStep(ST) <Int 0
    81	  rule slStart(someB(I:Int), ST:OptInt, LEN:Int)  => slAdjust(I, LEN, slStep(ST))
    82	
    83	  syntax Int ::= slStop(OptInt, OptInt, Int) [function]
    84	  rule slStop(noB,          ST:OptInt, LEN:Int)  => LEN
    85	       requires slStep(ST) >Int 0
    86	  rule slStop(noB,          ST:OptInt, _LEN:Int) => -1
    87	       requires slStep(ST) <Int 0
    88	  rule slStop(someB(I:Int), ST:OptInt, LEN:Int)  => slAdjust(I, LEN, slStep(ST))
    89	
    90	  syntax Int ::= slAdjust(Int, Int, Int) [function, total]
    91	  rule slAdjust(I:Int, LEN:Int, STEP:Int) => clampLo(I +Int LEN, STEP)
    92	       requires I  <Int 0
    93	  rule slAdjust(I:Int, LEN:Int, STEP:Int) => clampHi(I, LEN, STEP)
    94	       requires I >=Int 0
    95	
    96	  syntax Int ::= clampLo(Int, Int) [function, total]
    97	  rule clampLo(J:Int, _STEP:Int) => J
    98	       requires J >=Int 0
    99	  rule clampLo(J:Int, STEP:Int)  => #if STEP <Int 0 #then -1 #else 0 #fi
   100	       requires J <Int 0
   101	
   102	  syntax Int ::= clampHi(Int, Int, Int) [function, total]
   103	  rule clampHi(I:Int, LEN:Int, _STEP:Int) => I
   104	       requires I  <Int LEN
   105	  rule clampHi(I:Int, LEN:Int, STEP:Int)  => #if STEP <Int 0 #then LEN -Int 1 #else LEN #fi
   106	       requires I >=Int LEN
   107	
   108	  // ==== build the strided sub-sequence (indices in range by construction) ====
   109	  syntax ValSeq ::= buildVS(ValSeq, Int, Int, Int) [function]
   110	  rule buildVS(VS:ValSeq, I:Int, STOP:Int, STEP:Int)
   111	    => vCons(valSeqAt(VS, I), buildVS(VS, I +Int STEP, STOP, STEP))
   112	       requires (STEP >Int 0 andBool I <Int STOP) orBool (STEP <Int 0 andBool I >Int STOP)
   113	  rule buildVS(_:ValSeq, I:Int, STOP:Int, STEP:Int) => .ValSeq
   114	       requires notBool ((STEP >Int 0 andBool I <Int STOP) orBool (STEP <Int 0 andBool I >Int STOP))
   115	
   116	  syntax IntSeq ::= buildIS(IntSeq, Int, Int, Int) [function]
   117	  rule buildIS(IS:IntSeq, I:Int, STOP:Int, STEP:Int)
   118	    => iCons(intSeqAt(IS, I), buildIS(IS, I +Int STEP, STOP, STEP))
   119	       requires (STEP >Int 0 andBool I <Int STOP) orBool (STEP <Int 0 andBool I >Int STOP)
   120	  rule buildIS(_:IntSeq, I:Int, STOP:Int, STEP:Int) => .IntSeq
   121	       requires notBool ((STEP >Int 0 andBool I <Int STOP) orBool (STEP <Int 0 andBool I >Int STOP))
   122	endmodule

     3	module MPY-CONTROLS
     4	  imports MPY-CORE
     5	  imports MPY-TUPLE
     6	  imports MPY-ITER

     8	  // ==== Assign / AugAssign (write the current scope; RHS evaluated by strictness) ==
     9	  rule <k> Assign(Name(X:String), V:Val) => .K ... </k>
    10	       <env> L:Int </env>
    11	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map => M [ X <- V ], _) ... </scopes>
    12	  rule <k> Assign(Name(X:String), V:Val) => #cellW({M[X]}:>Val, V) ... </k>
    13	       <env> L:Int </env>
    14	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map, _) ... </scopes>
    15	       requires "$cells" in_keys(M)
    16	        andBool pnMember(X, cellsOf({M["$cells"]}:>Val))
    17	        andBool X in_keys(M) andBool isCellRef({M[X]}:>Val)
    18	       [priority(40)]
    19	
    20	  rule <k> AugAssign(Name(X:String), OP:String, V:Val) => .K ... </k>
    21	       <env> L:Int </env>
    22	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map => M [ X <- applyBin(OP, {M[X]}:>Val, V) ], _) ... </scopes>
    23	       requires X in_keys(M)
    24	  // `lst += [..]` where lst is a heap ref: the generic rule leaves applyBin(OP, ref, V) — but the
    25	  // ref-deref preemption is BinOp-level (operators.k), so applyBin never derefs and it sticks. Route
    26	  // the ref case through BinOp so the deref + list-concat + #alloc path fires (result is a fresh ref).
    27	  rule <k> AugAssign(Name(X:String), OP:String, V:Val) => Assign(Name(X), BinOp(OP, Name(X), V)) ... </k>
    28	       <env> L:Int </env>
    29	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map, _) ... </scopes>
    30	       requires X in_keys(M) andBool isRefV({M[X]}:>Val)
    31	       [priority(40)]
    32	
    33	  // ==== import trivia: `from math import floor, ceil` binds the supported
    34	  // names as builtins in the current scope; every other import is a no-op
    35	  rule <k> ImportFrom("math", NS:ParamNames) => #bindImports(NS) ... </k>
    36	  rule <k> ImportFrom(_:String, _:ParamNames) => .K ... </k> [owise]
    37	  syntax KItem ::= #bindImports(ParamNames)
    38	  rule <k> #bindImports(.ParamNames) => .K ... </k>
    39	  rule <k> #bindImports((N:String, NS:ParamNames)) => #bindImports(NS) ... </k>
    40	       <env> L:Int </env>
    41	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map => M [ N <- builtinV(N) ], _) ... </scopes>
    42	       requires N ==String "floor" orBool N ==String "ceil"
    43	  rule <k> #bindImports((N:String, NS:ParamNames)) => #bindImports(NS) ... </k>
    44	       requires notBool (N ==String "floor" orBool N ==String "ceil")

    46	  // ==== Expr statement: evaluate for effect, discard the value ===============
    47	  // (bare calls — mutator methods, docstrings; the WP0 statement-trivia rung)
    48	  rule <k> Expr(_:Val) => .K ... </k>

    50	  // ==== If (condition evaluated by strictness) ==============================
    51	  syntax KItem ::= #branch(Bool, Stmts, Stmts)
    52	  rule <k> If(C:Val, T:Stmts, E:Stmts) => #branch(truthy(C), T, E) ... </k>
    53	  rule <k> #branch(true,  T:Stmts, _:Stmts) => T ... </k>
    54	  rule <k> #branch(false, _:Stmts, E:Stmts) => E ... </k>

    62	  // ==== For: one loop, in-cell continuation, over #iterNext =================
    63	  // (the iterable is evaluated once, by strictness; the protocol stays rewrites —
    64	  // circularities anchor on #loop and narrowing substitutes the structure)
    65	  syntax KItem ::= #loop(Val, Expr, Stmts) | #loopStep(Expr, Stmts)
    66	                 | #while(Expr, Stmts) | #whileCond(Expr, Stmts)
    67	                 | #loopLbl(K) | "#cont" | "#brk"
    68	
    69	  rule <k> For(T:Expr, OBJ:Val, B:Stmts) => #loop(OBJ, T, B) ... </k>
    70	
    71	  rule <k> #loop(IT:Iterable, T:Expr, B:Stmts) => #iterNext(IT) ~> #loopStep(T, B) ... </k>
    72	  rule <k> #iterDone ~> #loopStep(_:Expr, _:Stmts) => .K ... </k>
    73	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, REST:Iterable) ~> #loopStep(T:Expr, B:Stmts)

    75	
    76	  // ==== While ==============================================================
    77	  rule <k> While(C:Expr, B:Stmts) => #while(C, B) ... </k>
    78	  rule <k> #while(C:Expr, B:Stmts) => C ~> #whileCond(C, B) ... </k>
    79	  rule <k> V:Val ~> #whileCond(C:Expr, B:Stmts) => B ~> #loopLbl(#while(C, B)) ... </k>

    81	  rule <k> V:Val ~> #whileCond(_C:Expr, _B:Stmts) => .K ... </k>
    82	       requires notBool truthy(V)

    84	  // ==== loop control (break / continue) =====================================
    85	  rule <k> #loopLbl(NEXT:K) => NEXT ... </k>
    86	  rule <k> Continue => #cont ... </k>
    87	  rule <k> Break => #brk ... </k>
    88	  rule <k> #cont ~> #loopLbl(NEXT:K) => NEXT ... </k>
    89	  rule <k> #cont ~> (_:KItem => .K) ... </k> [owise]
    90	  rule <k> #brk ~> #loopLbl(_:K) => .K ... </k>
    91	  rule <k> #brk ~> (_:KItem => .K) ... </k> [owise]
    92	
    93	  // ==== heap-object deref at the truthiness/iteration consumers ==============

    95	  rule <k> If(ref(H:Int), T:Stmts, E:Stmts) => If(V, T, E) ... </k>
    96	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    97	       [priority(40)]
    98	  rule <k> IfExp(ref(H:Int), T:Expr, E:Expr) => IfExp(V, T, E) ... </k>
    99	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
   100	       [priority(40)]
   101	  rule <k> ref(H:Int) ~> #whileCond(C:Expr, B:Stmts) => V ~> #whileCond(C, B) ... </k>
   102	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
   103	       [priority(40)]
   104	  // For derefs its iterable ONCE at loop start (iteration is over the snapshot;
   105	  // mutating the iterated list inside its own loop is outside the subset)
   106	  rule <k> For(T:Expr, ref(H:Int), B:Stmts) => For(T, V, B) ... </k>
   107	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
   108	       [priority(40)]

     8	  syntax KItem ::= #iterNext(Iterable) | "#iterDone" | #iterYield(Val, Iterable)
     9	endmodule

===== reference-semantics/semantics/range.k =====
     1	// reference/src/semantics/range.k — MPY-RANGE
     2	// rangeObj: the range helpers (inRange / rangeLen) + its #iterNext case. rangeObj itself is
     3	// declared in MPY-CORE's Iterable union; this module owns its behavior.
     4	
     5	module MPY-RANGE
     6	  imports MPY-CORE
     7	  imports MPY-ITER
     8	
     9	  syntax Bool ::= inRange(Int, Int, Int) [function, total]
    10	  rule inRange(I:Int, HI:Int, ST:Int) => (ST >Int 0 andBool I <Int HI) orBool (ST <Int 0 andBool I >Int HI)
    11	
    12	  syntax Int ::= rangeLen(Int, Int, Int) [function]
    13	  rule rangeLen(LO:Int, HI:Int, ST:Int) => (HI -Int LO +Int ST -Int 1) /Int ST
    14	       requires ST >Int 0 andBool HI >Int LO
    15	  rule rangeLen(LO:Int, HI:Int, ST:Int) => (LO -Int HI -Int ST -Int 1) /Int (0 -Int ST)
    16	       requires ST <Int 0 andBool HI <Int LO
    17	  rule rangeLen(LO:Int, HI:Int, ST:Int) => 0
    18	       requires (ST >Int 0 andBool HI <=Int LO) orBool (ST <Int 0 andBool HI >=Int LO)
    19	
    20	  rule <k> #iterNext(rangeObj(I:Int, HI:Int, ST:Int))
    21	        => #iterYield(I, rangeObj(I +Int ST, HI, ST)) ... </k>
    22	       requires inRange(I, HI, ST)
    23	  rule <k> #iterNext(rangeObj(I:Int, HI:Int, ST:Int)) => #iterDone ... </k>
    24	       requires notBool inRange(I, HI, ST)
    25	endmodule

===== reference-semantics/semantics/list.k =====
     1	// reference/src/semantics/list.k — MPY-LIST
     2	
     3	module MPY-LIST
     4	  imports MPY-CORE
     5	  imports MPY-ITER
     6	  imports MPY-OPERATORS
     7	
     8	  // ==== iteration (the iterator protocol's list case) =======================
     9	  rule <k> #iterNext(list(.ValSeq))                => #iterDone ... </k>
    10	  rule <k> #iterNext(list(vCons(V:Val, R:ValSeq))) => #iterYield(V, list(R)) ... </k>
    11	
    12	  // ==== ListExpr: [...] literal -> a fresh heap object =======================
    13	  syntax ApplyK ::= "toList"
    14	  rule <k> ListExpr(ES:Exprs) => #evalArgs(ES, .Vals, toList) ... </k>
    15	  rule <k> #applyK(toList, ACC:Vals) => #alloc(list(vals2valSeq(ACC))) ... </k>
    16	
    17	  // ==== list ops: + / == / != ===============================================
    18	  syntax ValSeq ::= valSeqConcat(ValSeq, ValSeq) [function, total]
    19	  rule valSeqConcat(.ValSeq, T:ValSeq)                => T
    20	  rule valSeqConcat(vCons(V:Val, S:ValSeq), T:ValSeq) => vCons(V, valSeqConcat(S, T))
    21	
    22	  // list + list constructs a NEW object (k-cell — it allocates; operands land here
    23	  // already deref'd). priority(45) beats the generic BinOp dispatch.
    24	  rule <k> BinOp("+", list(A:ValSeq), list(B:ValSeq)) => #alloc(list(valSeqConcat(A, B))) ... </k>
    25	       [priority(45)]
    26	
    27	  rule applyCmp("==", list(A:ValSeq), list(B:ValSeq)) => A ==K B
    28	  rule applyCmp("!=", list(A:ValSeq), list(B:ValSeq)) => notBool (A ==K B)
    29	
    30	  // ==== deep equality when elements are heap objects (list-of-lists) ========
    31	  // Python == is structural at every depth. Fires ONLY when a ref is present
    32	  // (the guard decides on concrete seqs); the plain ==K path above is unchanged.
    33	  syntax Bool ::= hasRefVS(ValSeq) [function, total]
    34	  rule hasRefVS(.ValSeq)                => false
    35	  rule hasRefVS(vCons(V:Val, R:ValSeq)) => isRefV(V) orBool hasRefVS(R)
    36	
    37	  syntax Bool ::= deepEqVS(ValSeq, ValSeq, Map) [function]
    38	                | deepEqV(Val, Val, Map)        [function]
    39	  rule deepEqVS(.ValSeq, .ValSeq, _:Map)                   => true
    40	  rule deepEqVS(.ValSeq, vCons(_:Val, _:ValSeq), _:Map)    => false
    41	  rule deepEqVS(vCons(_:Val, _:ValSeq), .ValSeq, _:Map)    => false
    42	  rule deepEqVS(vCons(A:Val, As:ValSeq), vCons(B:Val, Bs:ValSeq), HP:Map)
    43	    => deepEqV(A, B, HP) andBool deepEqVS(As, Bs, HP)
    44	
    45	  rule deepEqV(ref(H:Int), B:Val, HP:Map) => deepEqV({HP[H]}:>Val, B, HP)
    46	       requires H in_keys(HP)
    47	  rule deepEqV(A:Val, ref(H:Int), HP:Map) => deepEqV(A, {HP[H]}:>Val, HP)
    48	       requires notBool isRefV(A) andBool H in_keys(HP)
    49	  rule deepEqV(list(A:ValSeq), list(B:ValSeq), HP:Map) => deepEqVS(A, B, HP)
    50	  rule deepEqV(A:Val, B:Val, _:Map) => A ==K B [owise]
    51	
    52	  // ==== mutator: xs.append(v) — an in-place heap write ======================
    53	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(boundMethodV(ref(H:Int), "append")), (V:Val, .Vals)) => noneV ... </k>
    54	       <heap> ... H |-> list(VS:ValSeq => valSeqConcat(VS, vCons(V, .ValSeq))) ... </heap>
    55	       [priority(40)]
    56	
    57	  // ==== `x in list` — a <k>-cell fold over #iterNext ========================
    58	  syntax KItem ::= #memberAcc(Val, Iterable) | #memberCont(Val) | "#notB"
    59	  rule <k> Compare(LV:Val, CmpOp("in",     list(VS:ValSeq))) => #memberAcc(LV, list(VS)) ... </k>
    60	  rule <k> Compare(LV:Val, CmpOp("not in", list(VS:ValSeq))) => #memberAcc(LV, list(VS)) ~> #notB ... </k>
    61	  rule <k> #memberAcc(V:Val, IT:Iterable) => #iterNext(IT) ~> #memberCont(V) ... </k>
    62	  rule <k> #iterDone ~> #memberCont(_V:Val) => false ... </k>
    63	  rule <k> #iterYield(E:Val, _:Iterable) ~> #memberCont(V:Val) => true ... </k>
    64	       requires E ==K V
    65	  rule <k> #iterYield(E:Val, R:Iterable) ~> #memberCont(V:Val) => #memberAcc(V, R) ... </k>
    66	       requires notBool (E ==K V)
    67	  rule <k> B:Bool ~> #notB => notBool B ... </k>
    68	endmodule

===== reference-semantics/semantics/set.k =====
     1	// reference/src/semantics/set.k — MPY-SET
     2	
     3	module MPY-SET
     4	  imports MPY-CORE
     5	
     6	  // a set value, carried as its distinct codes in first-seen order (order is irrelevant
     7	  // to membership/cardinality — the two observations sets support here).
     8	  syntax Val ::= setV(IntSeq)
     9	
    10	  // membership of a code in the accumulated distinct-code sequence
    11	  syntax Bool ::= codeIn(Int, IntSeq) [function, total]
    12	  rule codeIn(_:Int, .IntSeq)                => false
    13	  rule codeIn(C:Int, iCons(H:Int, T:IntSeq)) => C ==Int H orBool codeIn(C, T)
    14	
    15	  // the distinct codes of CS (insert-if-absent fold, first-seen order)
    16	  syntax IntSeq ::= dedupCodes(IntSeq)         [function, total]
    17	                  | dedupFrom(IntSeq, IntSeq)  [function, total]
    18	  rule dedupCodes(CS:IntSeq) => dedupFrom(CS, .IntSeq)
    19	  rule dedupFrom(.IntSeq, ACC:IntSeq) => ACC
    20	  rule dedupFrom(iCons(C:Int, S:IntSeq), ACC:IntSeq) => dedupFrom(S, ACC)
    21	       requires codeIn(C, ACC)
    22	  rule dedupFrom(iCons(C:Int, S:IntSeq), ACC:IntSeq) => dedupFrom(S, snocCode(ACC, C))
    23	       requires notBool codeIn(C, ACC)
    24	
    25	  syntax IntSeq ::= snocCode(IntSeq, Int) [function, total]
    26	  rule snocCode(.IntSeq, C:Int)                => iCons(C, .IntSeq)
    27	  rule snocCode(iCons(H:Int, T:IntSeq), C:Int) => iCons(H, snocCode(T, C))
    28	
    29	  // ==== set equality: two sets are equal iff mutually subsuming ==============
    30	  // subsetCodes(A, B) — every code of A occurs in B (duplicates in A are harmless).
    31	  syntax Bool ::= subsetCodes(IntSeq, IntSeq) [function, total]
    32	  rule subsetCodes(.IntSeq, _:IntSeq)                => true
    33	  rule subsetCodes(iCons(C:Int, S:IntSeq), B:IntSeq) => codeIn(C, B) andBool subsetCodes(S, B)
    34	
    35	  syntax Bool ::= sameSet(IntSeq, IntSeq) [function, total]
    36	  rule sameSet(A:IntSeq, B:IntSeq) => subsetCodes(A, B) andBool subsetCodes(B, A)
    37	
    38	  // set == set  (the only comparison sets support here)
    39	  rule applyCmp("==", setV(A:IntSeq), setV(B:IntSeq)) => sameSet(A, B)
    40	endmodule

===== reference-semantics/semantics/dict.k =====
     1	// reference/src/semantics/dict.k — MPY-DICT
     2	//
     3	// Minimal dict support. A dict value is `dictV(KS, VS)`: PARALLEL insertion-ordered key/value
     4	// ValSeqs (Python dict order; keys distinct; re-inserting a key updates its value in place, keeping
     5	// the original position). Concrete for krun (the ordered build + `.keys()` are the real ops); a proof
     6	// over a SYMBOLIC dict passes `dictV(KS, WS)` with a symbolic key sequence KS and reads
     7	// `d.keys() = list(KS)`, then keeps each key opaque problem-locally.
     8	//
     9	// Only the pieces needed so far: a dict VALUE (so `{}` inside a mixed list evaluates and
    10	// `isinstance(x, int)` rejects it), the `{k: v, ...}` literal, and `.keys()`. More dict ops (subscript
    11	// / `.get()` / `.values()` / dict `==`) are added as dict problems need them — kept minimal + additive.
    12	
    13	module MPY-DICT
    14	  imports MPY-CORE
    15	  imports MPY-ITER
    16	  imports MPY-METHODS
    17	  imports MPY-LIST
    18	
    19	  // dict as PARALLEL ordered key/value ValSeqs (same length; keys distinct).
    20	  syntax Val ::= dictV(ValSeq, ValSeq)
    21	
    22	  // ==== DictExpr: {k: v, ...} literal. Eval each key then value, left to right, insert-with-dedup.
    23	  syntax KItem ::= #dictAcc(Entries, ValSeq, ValSeq)
    24	                 | #dictKey(Expr, Entries, ValSeq, ValSeq)
    25	                 | #dictVal(Val, Entries, ValSeq, ValSeq)
    26	  rule <k> DictExpr(ES:Entries) => #dictAcc(ES, .ValSeq, .ValSeq) ... </k>
    27	  rule <k> #dictAcc(.Entries, KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq) => dictV(KS, VS) ... </k>
    28	  rule <k> #dictAcc((Entry(K:Expr, V:Expr), REST:Entries), KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq)
    29	        => K ~> #dictKey(V, REST, KS, VS) ... </k>
    30	  rule <k> KV:Val ~> #dictKey(V:Expr, REST:Entries, KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq)
    31	        => V ~> #dictVal(KV, REST, KS, VS) ... </k>
    32	  rule <k> VV:Val ~> #dictVal(KV:Val, REST:Entries, KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq)
    33	        => #dictAcc(REST, dPutK(KS, KV), dPutV(KS, VS, KV, VV)) ... </k>
    34	
    35	  // insert-with-dedup helpers (concrete Val key equality via ==K). [total] so buildFold over a dict is
    36	  // total (its #Ceil is #Top) — needed when a symbolic proof carries a built dict as a config value.
    37	  syntax Bool ::= dHasKey(ValSeq, Val) [function, total]
    38	  rule dHasKey(.ValSeq, _:Val)                => false
    39	  rule dHasKey(vCons(A:Val, _:ValSeq), K:Val) => true          requires A ==K K
    40	  rule dHasKey(vCons(A:Val, R:ValSeq), K:Val) => dHasKey(R, K) requires notBool (A ==K K)
    41	
    42	  // dPutK: KS unchanged if K already present, else append K (keep-first-position).
    43	  syntax ValSeq ::= dPutK(ValSeq, Val) [function, total]
    44	  rule dPutK(KS:ValSeq, K:Val) => KS                                  requires dHasKey(KS, K)
    45	  rule dPutK(KS:ValSeq, K:Val) => valSeqConcat(KS, vCons(K, .ValSeq)) requires notBool dHasKey(KS, K)
    46	
    47	  // dPutV: parallel to KS — set the value at K's position if present, else append V at the end. The
    48	  // [owise] catch-all covers the degenerate mismatched-length case (never reached for a well-formed dict).
    49	  syntax ValSeq ::= dPutV(ValSeq, ValSeq, Val, Val) [function, total]
    50	  rule dPutV(vCons(A:Val, _:ValSeq), vCons(_:Val, VR:ValSeq), K:Val, V:Val)  => vCons(V, VR)
    51	       requires A ==K K
    52	  rule dPutV(vCons(A:Val, KR:ValSeq), vCons(B:Val, VR:ValSeq), K:Val, V:Val) => vCons(B, dPutV(KR, VR, K, V))
    53	       requires notBool (A ==K K)
    54	  rule dPutV(_KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq, _K:Val, V:Val) => valSeqConcat(VS, vCons(V, .ValSeq)) [owise]
    55	
    56	  // ==== dict methods ========================================================
    57	  // d.keys() -> a FRESH list object of the ordered keys (k-cell: it allocates).
    58	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(boundMethodV(dictV(KS:ValSeq, _:ValSeq), "keys")), .Vals)
    59	        => #alloc(list(KS)) ... </k>
    60	       [priority(40)]
    61	
    62	  // ==== dict subscript READ: d[k] (assoc lookup; KeyError is out of subset) ==
    63	  rule applyIndexD(dictV(KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq), K:Val) => dGet(KS, VS, K)
    64	  syntax Val ::= applyIndexD(Val, Val) [function]
    65	  rule <k> Subscript(dictV(KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq), K:Val) => applyIndexD(dictV(KS, VS), K) ... </k>
    66	       [priority(45)]
    67	
    68	  // ==== dict subscript-assign: d[k] = v (insert/update in place) =============
    69	  // Only for a LOCAL dict variable X (the current scope holds it). Reuses dPutK/dPutV.
    70	  syntax Val ::= dictSet(Val, Val, Val) [function]
    71	  rule dictSet(dictV(KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq), K:Val, V:Val) => dictV(dPutK(KS, K), dPutV(KS, VS, K, V))
    72	
    73	  // RHS evaluates first (Assign strictness), then the key. Dispatch on the scope
    74	  // value: a bare dict updates in the scope (dicts stay values); a ref (a heap
    75	  // list — or a heap dict later) writes the heap in place.
    76	  syntax KItem ::= #dsetK(String, Val)
    77	  rule <k> Assign(Subscript(Name(X:String), K:Expr), VV:Val) => K ~> #dsetK(X, VV) ... </k>
    78	  rule <k> KV:Val ~> #dsetK(X:String, VV:Val) => .K ... </k>
    79	       <env> L:Int </env>
    80	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map => M [ X <- dictSet({M[X]}:>Val, KV, VV) ], _) ... </scopes>
    81	       requires X in_keys(M) andBool notBool isRefV({M[X]}:>Val)
    82	  rule <k> KV:Val ~> #dsetK(X:String, VV:Val) => #dsetV({M[X]}:>Val, KV, VV) ... </k>
    83	       <env> L:Int </env>
    84	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map, _) ... </scopes>
    85	       requires X in_keys(M) andBool isRefV({M[X]}:>Val)
    86	  syntax KItem ::= #dsetV(Val, Val, Val)
    87	  rule <k> #dsetV(ref(H:Int), I:Int, VV:Val) => .K ... </k>
    88	       <heap> ... H |-> list(VS:ValSeq => setVSAt(VS, normIdxD(I, vsLen(VS)), VV)) ... </heap>
    89	  // negative-index normalization local to the write (subscript.k's is not imported here)
    90	  syntax Int ::= normIdxD(Int, Int) [function, total]
    91	  rule normIdxD(I:Int, LEN:Int) => I +Int LEN requires I  <Int 0
    92	  rule normIdxD(I:Int, _:Int)   => I          requires I >=Int 0
    93	
    94	  // ==== dict == (order-insensitive: same size + same key->value pairs) =======
    95	  rule applyCmp("==", dictV(KS1:ValSeq, VS1:ValSeq), dictV(KS2:ValSeq, VS2:ValSeq))
    96	    => (vsLen(KS1) ==Int vsLen(KS2)) andBool dSubset(KS1, VS1, KS2, VS2)
    97	  syntax Bool ::= dSubset(ValSeq, ValSeq, ValSeq, ValSeq) [function]
    98	  rule dSubset(.ValSeq, .ValSeq, _:ValSeq, _:ValSeq) => true
    99	  rule dSubset(vCons(K:Val, KR:ValSeq), vCons(V:Val, VR:ValSeq), KS2:ValSeq, VS2:ValSeq)
   100	    => dHasKey(KS2, K) andBool (dGet(KS2, VS2, K) ==K V) andBool dSubset(KR, VR, KS2, VS2)
   101	  syntax Val ::= dGet(ValSeq, ValSeq, Val) [function]
   102	  rule dGet(vCons(A:Val, _:ValSeq), vCons(B:Val, _:ValSeq), K:Val) => B                requires A ==K K
   103	  rule dGet(vCons(A:Val, KR:ValSeq), vCons(_:Val, VR:ValSeq), K:Val) => dGet(KR, VR, K) requires notBool (A ==K K)
   104	endmodule

     1	// reference/src/semantics/comprehension.k — MPY-COMPREHENSION

     3	module MPY-COMPREHENSION

     5	  imports MPY-OPERATORS

     7	  imports MPY-CONTROLS

    10	  // A comprehension is pure syntactic sugar

    12	  rule GenExp(ELT:Expr, Gs:CompFors)   => Call(closureExpr(.ParamNames, compBody(Gs, ELT)), .Exprs)

===== reference-semantics/semantics/sort.k =====
     1	// reference/src/semantics/sort.k — MPY-SORT
     2	// Trusted sorted(): sorted(list) as an opaque ascending permutation `sortVS` — opaque symbolic
     3	// for kprove (a trusted primitive, correctness/ordering proved in Lean / notes/sort-probe),
     4	// and a concrete insertion sort for krun. Wrappers verify the logic AROUND the sort (index /
     5	// slice / filter / dedup); indexing an opaque sortVS(VS) carries through as an opaque term, so
     6	// no ordering lemma is needed in K — the trust (sortVS = real sorted) is discharged by each
     7	// problem's differential test. Only int lists (compared by projectIntTotal); keyed / string
     8	// sorts are separate. Fires only via the "sorted" builtin, so inert for non-sorting programs.
     9	
    10	module MPY-SORT
    11	  imports MPY-BUILTINS
    12	  imports MPY-SUBSCRIPT
    13	
    14	  // sortVS(VS): the ascending sort of the Val list VS. Opaque for symbolic VS (no-evaluators);
    15	  // concrete insertion sort for krun.
    16	  // Concrete sort matches Int-sorted elements directly (an int Val IS an Int); projectIntTotal
    17	  // (lemmas-only) is not available in the semantics. Int and str lists.
    18	  syntax ValSeq ::= sortVS(ValSeq) [function, total, symbol(sortVS), no-evaluators]
    19	  syntax ValSeq ::= insVS(Int, ValSeq) [function]
    20	  rule sortVS(.ValSeq)                => .ValSeq          [concrete]
    21	  rule sortVS(vCons(X:Int, R:ValSeq)) => insVS(X, sortVS(R)) [concrete]
    22	  rule insVS(X:Int, .ValSeq)                => vCons(X, .ValSeq) [concrete]
    23	  rule insVS(X:Int, vCons(Y:Int, R:ValSeq)) => vCons(X, vCons(Y, R)) requires X <=Int Y [concrete]
    24	  rule insVS(X:Int, vCons(Y:Int, R:ValSeq)) => vCons(Y, insVS(X, R)) requires X  >Int Y [concrete]
    25	  // str elements insert by the shared lexicographic strLt (methods.k)
    26	  syntax ValSeq ::= insVSs(IntSeq, ValSeq) [function]
    27	  rule sortVS(vCons(str(CS:IntSeq), R:ValSeq)) => insVSs(CS, sortVS(R)) [concrete]
    28	  rule insVSs(A:IntSeq, .ValSeq) => vCons(str(A), .ValSeq) [concrete]
    29	  rule insVSs(A:IntSeq, vCons(str(B:IntSeq), R:ValSeq)) => vCons(str(A), vCons(str(B), R))
    30	       requires strLt(A, B) orBool A ==K B [concrete]
    31	  rule insVSs(A:IntSeq, vCons(str(B:IntSeq), R:ValSeq)) => vCons(str(B), insVSs(A, R))
    32	       requires notBool (strLt(A, B) orBool A ==K B) [concrete]
    33	
    34	  // sorted(list) constructs a NEW object: k-cell pre-dispatch (beats the [owise]
    35	  // applyBuiltin routing in call.k) so the result allocates.
    36	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(builtinV("sorted")), (list(VS:ValSeq), .Vals))
    37	        => #alloc(list(sortVS(VS))) ... </k>
    38	
    39	  // mutator: xs.sort() — the in-place heap write over the same trusted sortVS
    40	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(boundMethodV(ref(H:Int), "sort")), .Vals) => noneV ... </k>
    41	       <heap> ... H |-> list(VS:ValSeq => sortVS(VS)) ... </heap>
    42	       [priority(40)]
    43	
    44	  // ==== keyed / reversed sorted() (WP2) =====================================
    45	  // sortKeyVS(VS, KV): the stable ascending sort of VS by the key value KV
    46	  // (a closure/builtin/type — anything callable). OPAQUE here; the concrete
    47	  // leg (MPY-CONCRETE, llvm only) computes keys by REAL calls and stable-
    48	  // inserts, at priority(40) over these.
    49	  syntax ValSeq ::= sortKeyVS(ValSeq, Val) [function, total, symbol(sortKeyVS), no-evaluators]
    50	
    51	  syntax ValSeq ::= revVS(ValSeq) [function, total]
    52	                  | revVSAcc(ValSeq, ValSeq) [function, total]
    53	  rule revVS(S:ValSeq) => revVSAcc(S, .ValSeq)
    54	  rule revVSAcc(.ValSeq, A:ValSeq) => A
    55	  rule revVSAcc(vCons(V:Val, R:ValSeq), A:ValSeq) => revVSAcc(R, vCons(V, A))
    56	
    57	  syntax ValSeq ::= condRev(ValSeq, Bool) [function, total]
    58	  rule condRev(S:ValSeq, false) => S
    59	  rule condRev(S:ValSeq, true)  => revVS(S)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Mechanical checks over the proof-local BF-VERIFICATION theory."""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from pathlib import Path


SCRATCH = Path("/tmp/audit-work/148-bf-audit")
VERIFICATION = SCRATCH / "verification.k"
PLANET_CTORS = [
    "pMercury",
    "pVenus",
    "pEarth",
    "pMars",
    "pJupiter",
    "pSaturn",
    "pUranus",
    "pNeptune",
]


def main() -> None:
    text = VERIFICATION.read_text()

    assert "claim" not in text
    for forbidden in ["simplification", "no-evaluators", "[owise]", "priority("]:
        assert forbidden not in text, forbidden

    total_declarations = re.findall(
        r"^\s*syntax\s+.*?\[([^\]]*\btotal\b[^\]]*)\]",
        text,
        flags=re.MULTILINE,
    )
    assert len(total_declarations) == 4
    assert "planetVals" in text
    assert "expectedBetween(Int, Int)" in text
    assert "planetCodes(Planet)" in text
    assert "planetPosition(Planet)" in text

    for ctor in PLANET_CTORS:

*** Add File: /audit-output/REVIEW.md
+# Independent adversarial audit — 148-bf
+
+The candidate contains a legitimate partial-correctness proof for the submitted
+program under the supplied semantics. I reconstructed the definitions from
+source, obtained a fresh `#Top`, mechanically pinned the proof term to the
+translated program body, reviewed all source-level K entries, and obtained the
+expected failures from both a false-result mutation and an executed-body
+mutation.
+
+## 1. Input and provenance integrity
+
+The launcher record declares `record_layout: pipeline-v3`,
+`condition: semantics`, and `semantics_mode: SUPPLIED_SEMANTICS`.
+`/reference/reference-semantics` is present, as required for that mode.
+
+I read `/audit-input.json`, `/audit-campaign-lock.json`, `/run.json`,
+`/task.json`, `/generation-result.json`, all seven required files at the root of
+`/generation-evidence`, and all 622 JSON records in the single structured trace
+file. The generation prose, transcript, compiled directories, and prior
+`KPROVE_PASSED` assertion were treated only as untrusted historical claims.
+
+Independent checks found:
+
+- `/audit-campaign-lock.json` is JSON-equal to the `audit_campaign` block and
+  its SHA-256 is the recorded
+  `ad5dfcc006af70c4d0d2c6641f0878a6c54a266e9ad2b54cd225b2381a78d745`.
+- Every pipeline-v3 required record is a regular readable file or directory of
+  the expected kind. The trace has one regular JSONL file and no malformed
+  record.
+- The recorded SHA-256 values for the run/task/result/invocation manifests,
+  prompt, metrics, runtime metrics, usage, transcript, final message, trusted
+  canonical, prompt, and translator all equal hashes independently computed
+  from the mounted files.
+- Candidate `prompt.py` and `py2mpy.py` are byte-identical to the trusted
+  mounts.
+- Candidate `reference-semantics/` and trusted
+  `/reference/reference-semantics/` have exactly the same 25-entry recursive
+  manifest, types, paths, sizes, and file hashes. Neither tree contains a
+  symlink. The reviewer-defined manifest digest for either tree is
+  `a672ebc5644e3ffe3d963c31999f660850e86840b0c497807fea7c85e6706751`.
+- All required proof artifacts—`solution.py`, `solution.mpy`,
+  `verification.k`, `spec.k`, and `prove.sh`—are regular files.
+
+The complete checker and transcript are
+[provenance_check.py](/audit-output/evidence/provenance_check.py) and
+[stage1-provenance-final.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage1-provenance-final.log).
+The earlier `stage1-provenance.log` records a reviewer-script comparison error:
+the embedded task block has a launcher-added `config` key absent from
+`/task.json`. Correcting that reviewer-only comparison produced the clean run;
+it was not a mount or candidate discrepancy.
+
+There is no audit-infrastructure breach.
+
+## 2. Program fidelity and candidate-versus-canonical checks
+
+The trusted contract asks for `bf(planet1, planet2)` on string inputs. The
+planet order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
+For two valid names, the result must be the tuple of planets strictly between
+them in solar order. If either name is invalid, the result must be empty.
+Equal valid names consequently have no planet strictly between them.
+
+The trusted canonical implementation explicitly rejects equal names, looks up
+the two indices, and returns the corresponding open slice. The candidate omits
+the explicit equality test; its reversed/equal branch evaluates
+`planets[second + 1:first]`, which is empty when the indices are equal. Thus the
+two implementations agree on that boundary.
+
+Running the trusted translator over the mounted `solution.py` recreated the
+submitted `solution.mpy` byte-for-byte. Both SHA-256 values are
+`3f657ffd4d066c0d77ca1927b490720f80cac27830b713caaf4bdf9cfee6a7fa`;
+see [stage2-regeneration.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage2-regeneration.log).
+
+The independent differential test imports both entry points and also uses a
+third, index-free contract oracle. Its 939 unique string pairs include:
+
+- all three documented examples;
+- all 64 ordered pairs of valid names, including equal, adjacent, first/last,
+  and both orderings;
+- empty, case-shifted, whitespace-adjacent, NUL-containing, and Unicode
+  invalid strings in both argument positions; and
+- 200 deterministic generated invalid strings with seed 148.
+
+There were zero mismatches. The script and successful transcript are
+[differential_test.py](/audit-output/evidence/differential_test.py) and
+[stage2-differential-final.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage2-differential-final.log).
+The preserved first run found seven discrepancies caused by my oracle failing
+to special-case equal valid names; both Python implementations returned the
+correct empty tuple. I fixed the reviewer oracle and retained that diagnostic
+as `stage2-differential.log`.
+
+Program fidelity passes.
+
+## 3. Clean proof reconstruction
+
+I copied only candidate source artifacts and the trusted mounted inputs to
+`/tmp/audit-work/148-bf-audit`. I did not copy or use
+`/candidate/runtime-kompiled`, `/candidate/verification-kompiled`,
+`/candidate/__pycache__`, or any candidate cache.
+
+The active toolchain is K v7.1.293 and Python 3.10.12
+([stage0-toolchain.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage0-toolchain.log)).
+Fresh builds were:
+
+```text
+kompile reference-semantics/semantics.k --backend llvm \
+  --main-module MPY-KRUN --syntax-module MPY-SYNTAX \
+  --output-definition reviewer-runtime-kompiled
+
+kompile verification.k --backend haskell \
+  --main-module BF-VERIFICATION --syntax-module BF-VERIFICATION \
+  --output-definition reviewer-verification-kompiled
+```
+
+Both exited 0. Logs are
+[stage3-kompile-llvm.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage3-kompile-llvm.log) and
+[stage3-kompile-haskell.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage3-kompile-haskell.log).
+
+The original positive target command was then run unchanged except for the
+fresh definition name:
+
+```text
+kprove spec.k --definition reviewer-verification-kompiled \
+  --spec-module BF-SPEC
+```
+
+It processed all three claims, exited 0, and printed `#Top`. The bounded
+transcript is
+[stage3-kprove-all.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage3-kprove-all.log).
+
+I also translated and ran an independently authored concrete program containing
+the submitted function plus ten normal/boundary assertions through the fresh
+LLVM definition. Python execution, translation, and `krun` all exited 0; see
+[stage3-concrete-tests.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage3-concrete-tests.log).
+
+The LLVM compiler warned that several supplied `[total]` functions are not
+constructor-exhaustive. This is addressed under Stages 5 and 7; it did not
+prevent either fresh build or touch an unconstrained case in this proof.
+
+Clean reconstruction passes.
+
+## 4. Adequacy and real-program pinning
+
+### Claim meanings and coverage
+
+The first entry claim starts at `#validCases(0, 0)` in the ordinary initial
+configuration. Three disjoint controller rules traverse
+
+```text
+(0,0), (0,1), ... (0,7), (1,0), ... , (7,7)
+```
+
+exactly once. At each of the 64 states it calls the submitted function body on
+the corresponding valid names and executes a real `Assert` comparing the
+return to the explicit open interval in the eight-planet sequence. The claim's
+destination requires `.K`, `NoExc`, and exit code 0. A false assertion changes
+the latter two cells, so this is result-constraining even though 64 return
+checks are combined into one reachability claim.
+
+The second entry claim quantifies over arbitrary `IntSeq` values `A` and `_B`.
+Its precondition says `A` differs from every valid planet encoding. It proves
+that calling the body on `str(A), str(_B)` returns the empty tuple. This covers
+every first-invalid string and relies on the program's real short-circuiting,
+which correctly makes the second value irrelevant.
+
+The third entry claim says `A` equals one of the eight valid encodings while
+`B` differs from all eight. It proves the same empty tuple for every
+valid-first/invalid-second string pair.
+
+These domains are exhaustive for the contract's string inputs:
+
+```text
+both valid (8 × 8)  OR  first invalid  OR  first valid and second invalid.
+```
+
+The finite 64-case component is not a bounded approximation of an unrestricted
+valid domain: the source contract has exactly eight valid names. All remaining
+strings are covered symbolically rather than by examples.
+
+Each entry precondition has a concrete witness. The reviewer claims use
+Mercury/Neptune for the valid component, `""`/Neptune for first-invalid, and
+Earth/`""` for valid-first/second-invalid. They prove respectively the literal
+six-planet tuple and two literal empty tuples, print `#Top`, and exit 0
+([stage4-ground-witnesses.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage4-ground-witnesses.log)).
+The same results agree with both Python implementations in Stage 2.
+
+### Program identity
+
+Trusted regeneration establishes the `solution.py` to `solution.mpy` link. To
+check the next link mechanically, I extracted the sole translated function
+body using the trusted translator, parsed it as `Stmts`, expanded macros with
+the fresh definition, and compared its KORE to expanded `bfBody`. The KORE
+files are byte-identical and both hash to
+`644ce421a13ba7d711e970a2448745204080a98b6c33ca4a964b00488bb61d7d`;
+see [stage4-body-pinning.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage4-body-pinning.log).
+
+`bfRun` is a syntax macro, not an execution rewrite. Its closure has the exact
+source name-independent invocation data: parameters `planet1, planet2`, no
+remaining parameters, the identical `bfBody`, and definition scope 0. Under
+the fixed `FuncDef` rule, loading the actual module binds exactly
+`closureVal(Params, Body, 0)` in the initial module scope; `bfRun` directly
+constructs that same closure value. It then enters the ordinary fixed call,
+binding, body, return, and frame-pop rules. The proof therefore omits only
+module-load steps already accounted for by this mechanical constructor
+comparison; it does not substitute a different function or summary.
+
+As a separate body-sensitivity test, I changed the `"Earth"` literal in the
+executed `bfBody` to `"EarthX"` while leaving the result definition unchanged.
+The mutated definition built successfully, but its target proof exited 1 with
+`WarnStuckClaimState`, `AssertionError`, and exit code 1. See
+[stage4-body-mutation-kompile.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage4-body-mutation-kompile.log)
+and
+[stage4-body-mutation-proof.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage4-body-mutation-proof.log).
+This mutation changes the K term actually executed by the claim.
+
+Real-program pinning and adequacy pass.
+
+## 5. Rule-by-rule static soundness review
+
+The exhaustive inventory is
+[rule-inventory.tsv](/audit-output/evidence/rule-inventory.tsv), generated by
+[rule_inventory.py](/audit-output/evidence/rule_inventory.py). It contains 970
+source-level entries: 727 rules, 237 syntax declarations, five contexts, and
+one configuration. Every entry records its source and line, complete normalized
+text, attributes (`function`, `total`, `macro`, `priority`, `owise`,
+`concrete`, `no-evaluators`, and others), semantic role, and audit disposition.
+Per-file counts are in
+[rule-inventory-summary.txt](/audit-output/evidence/rule-inventory-summary.txt).
+
+### Used-constructor map
+
+| Submitted construct | Declaration and material rule families |
+|---|---|
+| `Module`, `FuncDef`, direct closure call | `syntax.k`; `core.k` load/sequence/lookup; `functions.k` define/bind/return/pop; `call.k` callee/arguments/closure dispatch |
+| `Assign`, `Name` | `syntax.k`; `controls.k` assignment; `core.k` lexical lookup |
+| `TupleExpr`, tuple membership/equality/index | `tuple.k`; shared argument evaluation in `core.k`; membership fold in `list.k` |
+| `Str`, arbitrary string values | `str.k` literal/code rules and structural equality |
+| `BoolOp("or")` | left-to-right contexts and disjoint truthy branches in `bool.k` |
+| `Compare("not in")`, integer `<` | `operators.k`, `tuple.k`, `list.k`, and `int.k` |
+| `Call(Attribute(..., "index"), ...)` | bound-method and argument routing in `call.k`; `idxOfVS` in `tuple.k` |
+| `Int`, `BinOp("+")`, `If` | `core.k`, `int.k`, and `controls.k` |
+| `Subscript(..., Slice(...))` | bound evaluation, clamping, and `buildVS` in `subscript.k` |
+| `Return` | strict value evaluation and frame restoration in `functions.k` |
+| proof-harness `Assert` | `assert.k`; failure changes `<exc>` and `<exit-code>` |
+
+The relevant rules preserve left-to-right evaluation, create one fresh function
+scope, bind the two parameters and locals there, read the immutable tuple
+structurally, and restore the initial environment/scope/stack/return cells on
+pop. Tuple literals and tuple slices are values, so this program performs no
+heap allocation. Membership and `idxOfVS` descend through ground
+constructor sequences. Slice bounds are ground non-negative indices in
+`0..7`, the step is `noB`/1, and every `valSeqAt` call made by `buildVS` is
+in-bounds.
+
+### Proof-local entries
+
+The local theory has:
+
+- `bfBody`, `bfCall`, and `bfRun` macros. `bfCall` is unused; `bfBody` and
+  `bfRun` are mechanically pinned as described above.
+- Four total mathematical definitions: nullary `planetVals`,
+  `expectedBetween(Int,Int)`, and exhaustive maps `planetCodes(Planet)` and
+  `planetPosition(Planet)`. The last two are unused by the final claims.
+- A finite eight-constructor `Planet` sort and eight ground `planetExpr`
+  equations. `planetExpr` is not declared total and is called only at its eight
+  defined ground arguments.
+- Three mutually exclusive `#validCases` rules. Their transition graph has
+  exactly 64 unique states and no gap or duplicate.
+
+There is no proof-local `claim`, simplification, priority, `owise`,
+`no-evaluators`, fresh opaque result, oracle, or rule that rewrites a submitted
+program operation to its answer. `expectedBetween` occurs only on the expected
+side of an assertion; it does not replace execution. `#validCases` is a fresh
+controller that schedules real body calls and assertions, and it reads/writes
+no program state beyond the standard `<k>` sequencing. Mechanical checks are
+in
+[proof_local_checks.py](/audit-output/evidence/proof_local_checks.py) and
+[stage5-proof-local-checks-final2.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage5-proof-local-checks-final2.log).
+
+The expected result reuses supplied `doSlice`, but this is not a circular
+proof-local abstraction: the candidate body still must compute the correct two
+indices, choose their order, and execute its own slice. Static inspection of
+the relevant supplied equations shows that for the only admitted domain
+(length 8, non-negative endpoints, step 1), `slStart`/`slStop` clamp correctly
+and `buildVS` returns exactly the strict open interval. The literal
+Mercury/Neptune witness independently fixes the six returned strings rather
+than leaving `doSlice` opaque.
+
+### Supplied-semantics boundary
+
+The imported fixed semantics contains opaque float/sort/digest symbols:
+`intFloatDiv`, `divII`, `floatMod`, `floatLt`, `absF`, `subF`, `divF`, `addF`,
+`mulF`, `powF`, `gtF`, `eqF`, `decStrToF`, `divFloatIntV`, `intToF`, `truncF`,
+`roundF`, `roundFN`, `sqrtF`, `sortVS`, `sortKeyVS`, and `md5hexCodes`. None
+appears in the program term, the expected result, a guard, or a claim.
+
+The LLVM warnings identify non-exhaustive total functions such as `mapStrVS`,
+`floorFI`, `toF`, `ceilF`, `joinCodes`, and `valSeqAt`. All but `valSeqAt` are
+outside the dynamic trust cone. `valSeqAt` is reached only on concrete
+nonempty `vCons` sequences at an in-bounds non-negative index, where an
+ordinary defining equation applies; the unconstrained total case is never
+used. Consequently these broad supplied declarations create no false
+conclusion witness for this theorem. I do not label them unsound merely from a
+global coverage warning; they are recorded as trust-boundary limitations.
+
+No inventoried proof-local or relevant supplied rule enables a false conclusion
+on the intended input domain. Static soundness passes.
+
+## 6. Fresh non-vacuity test
+
+I authored `spec-vacuity-reviewer.k` in scratch. It uses the concrete satisfying
+input Mercury/Neptune but falsely requires the empty tuple.
+
+The dry run parsed and built the claim successfully with exit 0
+([stage6-vacuity-dry-run.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage6-vacuity-dry-run.log)).
+The actual proof exited 1 with `WarnStuckClaimState`. Its residual displays the
+six actual values Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus against the false
+empty target
+([stage6-vacuity-proof.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage6-vacuity-proof.log)).
+
+This is a reachable, result-bearing failure, distinct from the executed-body
+mutation in Stage 4. Non-vacuity passes.
+
+## 7. Proven versus assumed accounting
+
+### What the K proof establishes
+
+Under the supplied semantics and the standard initial configuration, the exact
+submitted `bf` body has the following partial-correctness behavior for every
+pair of string values:
+
+- if both values are the encodings of valid planet names, the returned tuple is
+  exactly the planets strictly between them in the fixed solar order;
+- if either value is not a valid name, the returned tuple is empty; and
+- execution returns with the initial module environment restored, empty heap
+  and stack, `noRet`, `NoExc`, and exit code 0.
+
+The valid part is an exhaustive proof over the contract's finite 8×8 valid
+domain. The invalid part is symbolic over arbitrary `IntSeq` string contents.
+This is not merely differential testing and not merely the historical
+candidate `#Top`; it is the fresh reachability result in Stage 3.
+
+### Trust ledger
+
+| Boundary | Dependents | Assessment |
+|---|---|---|
+| K v7.1.293 parser/compiler, Haskell backend, reachability engine, SMT solver, and built-in integer/Boolean/String/Map/List hooks | All machine-checked claims | Necessary low-level proof-system trust; version and fresh outputs are recorded. |
+| Byte-identical supplied semantics | Meaning of calls, strings, tuples, control, slices, and assertions | Selected fixed-semantics boundary. All source entries were inventoried; the relevant trust cone was reviewed rule-by-rule. |
+| Trusted `py2mpy.py` | Source-to-`solution.mpy` link | Acceptable benchmark input. Byte regeneration and KORE body comparison independently check its use on this source. |
+| Direct-closure normalization in `bfRun` | All entry claims | Acceptable and mechanically justified: name/parameters/body/scope anchor equal the closure created by fixed module-load semantics. It skips no function-body operation. |
+| K `str(IntSeq)` representation of arbitrary Python strings | Symbolic invalid-input coverage | Non-fatal representation bridge. Valid literals are ASCII and ground; every other `IntSeq` is handled uniformly as invalid. Python Unicode/NUL cases were additionally tested, but finite tests are only evidence for this bridge. |
+| `planetVals`, min/max, and supplied ground slice equations as the natural-language “between” interpretation | Valid-pair postcondition | Ordinary finite mathematics, statically checked for all eight positions and backed by literal ground witness claims. No opaque answer symbol is involved. |
+| Imported float/sort/MD5 opaque symbols and unrelated broad total declarations | None of these claims | Inert. They affect neither control nor result and are not assumptions of this theorem. |
+| Python differential tests | Source/canonical agreement and representation evidence | Empirical support only; not used as a substitute for the K proof. |
+
+Gate A (real-program soundness and non-vacuity), Gate B (intent/domain
+adequacy), and Gate C (trust/evidence auditability) all pass. The full exact
+command index, including reviewer-script diagnostics and every exit status, is
+[COMMANDS.md](/audit-output/evidence/COMMANDS.md).
+
+VERDICT: PASS
+LEGITIMACY: LEGIT
*** End Patch

## 2. Program fidelity and candidate-versus-canonical checks

The trusted contract asks for `bf(planet1, planet2)` on string inputs. The
planet order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
For two valid names, the result must be the tuple of planets strictly between
them in solar order. If either name is invalid, the result must be empty.
Equal valid names consequently have no planet strictly between them.

The trusted canonical implementation explicitly rejects equal names, looks up
the two indices, and returns the corresponding open slice. The candidate omits
the explicit equality test; its reversed/equal branch evaluates
`planets[second + 1:first]`, which is empty when the indices are equal. Thus the
two implementations agree on that boundary.

Running the trusted translator over the mounted `solution.py` recreated the
submitted `solution.mpy` byte-for-byte. Both SHA-256 values are
`3f657ffd4d066c0d77ca1927b490720f80cac27830b713caaf4bdf9cfee6a7fa`;
see [stage2-regeneration.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage2-regeneration.log).

The independent differential test imports both entry points and also uses a
third, index-free contract oracle. Its 939 unique string pairs include:

- all three documented examples;
- all 64 ordered pairs of valid names, including equal, adjacent, first/last,
  and both orderings;
- empty, case-shifted, whitespace-adjacent, NUL-containing, and Unicode
  invalid strings in both argument positions; and
- 200 deterministic generated invalid strings with seed 148.

There were zero mismatches. The script and successful transcript are
[differential_test.py](/audit-output/evidence/differential_test.py) and
[stage2-differential-final.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage2-differential-final.log).
The preserved first run found seven discrepancies caused by my oracle failing
to special-case equal valid names; both Python implementations returned the
correct empty tuple. I fixed the reviewer oracle and retained that diagnostic
as `stage2-differential.log`.

Program fidelity passes.

([stage0-toolchain.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage0-toolchain.log)).

## 4. Adequacy and real-program pinning

### Claim meanings and coverage

The first entry claim starts at `#validCases(0, 0)` in the ordinary initial
configuration. Three disjoint controller rules traverse

```text
(0,0), (0,1), ... (0,7), (1,0), ... , (7,7)
```

exactly once. At each of the 64 states it calls the submitted function body on
the corresponding valid names and executes a real `Assert` comparing the
return to the explicit open interval in the eight-planet sequence. The claim's
destination requires `.K`, `NoExc`, and exit code 0. A false assertion changes
the latter two cells, so this is result-constraining even though 64 return
checks are combined into one reachability claim.

The second entry claim quantifies over arbitrary `IntSeq` values `A` and `_B`.
Its precondition says `A` differs from every valid planet encoding. It proves
that calling the body on `str(A), str(_B)` returns the empty tuple. This covers
every first-invalid string and relies on the program's real short-circuiting,
which correctly makes the second value irrelevant.

The third entry claim says `A` equals one of the eight valid encodings while
`B` differs from all eight. It proves the same empty tuple for every
valid-first/invalid-second string pair.

These domains are exhaustive for the contract's string inputs:

```text
both valid (8 × 8)  OR  first invalid  OR  first valid and second invalid.
```

The finite 64-case component is not a bounded approximation of an unrestricted
valid domain: the source contract has exactly eight valid names. All remaining
strings are covered symbolically rather than by examples.

Each entry precondition has a concrete witness. The reviewer claims use
Mercury/Neptune for the valid component, `""`/Neptune for first-invalid, and
Earth/`""` for valid-first/second-invalid. They prove respectively the literal
six-planet tuple and two literal empty tuples, print `#Top`, and exit 0
([stage4-ground-witnesses.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage4-ground-witnesses.log)).
The same results agree with both Python implementations in Stage 2.

### Program identity

Trusted regeneration establishes the `solution.py` to `solution.mpy` link. To
check the next link mechanically, I extracted the sole translated function
body using the trusted translator, parsed it as `Stmts`, expanded macros with
the fresh definition, and compared its KORE to expanded `bfBody`. The KORE
files are byte-identical and both hash to
`644ce421a13ba7d711e970a2448745204080a98b6c33ca4a964b00488bb61d7d`;
see [stage4-body-pinning.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage4-body-pinning.log).

`bfRun` is a syntax macro, not an execution rewrite. Its closure has the exact
source name-independent invocation data: parameters `planet1, planet2`, no
remaining parameters, the identical `bfBody`, and definition scope 0. Under
the fixed `FuncDef` rule, loading the actual module binds exactly
`closureVal(Params, Body, 0)` in the initial module scope; `bfRun` directly
constructs that same closure value. It then enters the ordinary fixed call,
binding, body, return, and frame-pop rules. The proof therefore omits only
module-load steps already accounted for by this mechanical constructor
comparison; it does not substitute a different function or summary.

As a separate body-sensitivity test, I changed the `"Earth"` literal in the
executed `bfBody` to `"EarthX"` while leaving the result definition unchanged.
The mutated definition built successfully, but its target proof exited 1 with
`WarnStuckClaimState`, `AssertionError`, and exit code 1. See
[stage4-body-mutation-kompile.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage4-body-mutation-kompile.log)
and
[stage4-body-mutation-proof.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage4-body-mutation-proof.log).
This mutation changes the K term actually executed by the claim.

Real-program pinning and adequacy pass.

## 5. Rule-by-rule static soundness review

The exhaustive inventory is
[rule-inventory.tsv](/audit-output/evidence/rule-inventory.tsv), generated by
[rule_inventory.py](/audit-output/evidence/rule_inventory.py). It contains 970
source-level entries: 727 rules, 237 syntax declarations, five contexts, and
one configuration. Every entry records its source and line, complete normalized
text, attributes (`function`, `total`, `macro`, `priority`, `owise`,
`concrete`, `no-evaluators`, and others), semantic role, and audit disposition.
Per-file counts are in
[rule-inventory-summary.txt](/audit-output/evidence/rule-inventory-summary.txt).

### Used-constructor map

| Submitted construct | Declaration and material rule families |
|---|---|
| `Module`, `FuncDef`, direct closure call | `syntax.k`; `core.k` load/sequence/lookup; `functions.k` define/bind/return/pop; `call.k` callee/arguments/closure dispatch |
| `Assign`, `Name` | `syntax.k`; `controls.k` assignment; `core.k` lexical lookup |
| `TupleExpr`, tuple membership/equality/index | `tuple.k`; shared argument evaluation in `core.k`; membership fold in `list.k` |
| `Str`, arbitrary string values | `str.k` literal/code rules and structural equality |
| `BoolOp("or")` | left-to-right contexts and disjoint truthy branches in `bool.k` |
| `Compare("not in")`, integer `<` | `operators.k`, `tuple.k`, `list.k`, and `int.k` |
| `Call(Attribute(..., "index"), ...)` | bound-method and argument routing in `call.k`; `idxOfVS` in `tuple.k` |
| `Int`, `BinOp("+")`, `If` | `core.k`, `int.k`, and `controls.k` |
| `Subscript(..., Slice(...))` | bound evaluation, clamping, and `buildVS` in `subscript.k` |
| `Return` | strict value evaluation and frame restoration in `functions.k` |
| proof-harness `Assert` | `assert.k`; failure changes `<exc>` and `<exit-code>` |

The relevant rules preserve left-to-right evaluation, create one fresh function
scope, bind the two parameters and locals there, read the immutable tuple
structurally, and restore the initial environment/scope/stack/return cells on
pop. Tuple literals and tuple slices are values, so this program performs no
heap allocation. Membership and `idxOfVS` descend through ground
constructor sequences. Slice bounds are ground non-negative indices in
`0..7`, the step is `noB`/1, and every `valSeqAt` call made by `buildVS` is
in-bounds.

### Proof-local entries

The local theory has:

- `bfBody`, `bfCall`, and `bfRun` macros. `bfCall` is unused; `bfBody` and
  `bfRun` are mechanically pinned as described above.
- Four total mathematical definitions: nullary `planetVals`,
  `expectedBetween(Int,Int)`, and exhaustive maps `planetCodes(Planet)` and
  `planetPosition(Planet)`. The last two are unused by the final claims.
- A finite eight-constructor `Planet` sort and eight ground `planetExpr`
  equations. `planetExpr` is not declared total and is called only at its eight
  defined ground arguments.
- Three mutually exclusive `#validCases` rules. Their transition graph has
  exactly 64 unique states and no gap or duplicate.

There is no proof-local `claim`, simplification, priority, `owise`,
`no-evaluators`, fresh opaque result, oracle, or rule that rewrites a submitted
program operation to its answer. `expectedBetween` occurs only on the expected
side of an assertion; it does not replace execution. `#validCases` is a fresh
controller that schedules real body calls and assertions, and it reads/writes
no program state beyond the standard `<k>` sequencing. Mechanical checks are
in
[proof_local_checks.py](/audit-output/evidence/proof_local_checks.py) and
[stage5-proof-local-checks-final2.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage5-proof-local-checks-final2.log).

The expected result reuses supplied `doSlice`, but this is not a circular
proof-local abstraction: the candidate body still must compute the correct two
indices, choose their order, and execute its own slice. Static inspection of
the relevant supplied equations shows that for the only admitted domain
(length 8, non-negative endpoints, step 1), `slStart`/`slStop` clamp correctly
and `buildVS` returns exactly the strict open interval. The literal
Mercury/Neptune witness independently fixes the six returned strings rather
than leaving `doSlice` opaque.

### Supplied-semantics boundary

The imported fixed semantics contains opaque float/sort/digest symbols:
`intFloatDiv`, `divII`, `floatMod`, `floatLt`, `absF`, `subF`, `divF`, `addF`,
`mulF`, `powF`, `gtF`, `eqF`, `decStrToF`, `divFloatIntV`, `intToF`, `truncF`,
`roundF`, `roundFN`, `sqrtF`, `sortVS`, `sortKeyVS`, and `md5hexCodes`. None
appears in the program term, the expected result, a guard, or a claim.

The LLVM warnings identify non-exhaustive total functions such as `mapStrVS`,
`floorFI`, `toF`, `ceilF`, `joinCodes`, and `valSeqAt`. All but `valSeqAt` are
outside the dynamic trust cone. `valSeqAt` is reached only on concrete
nonempty `vCons` sequences at an in-bounds non-negative index, where an
ordinary defining equation applies; the unconstrained total case is never
used. Consequently these broad supplied declarations create no false
conclusion witness for this theorem. I do not label them unsound merely from a
global coverage warning; they are recorded as trust-boundary limitations.

No inventoried proof-local or relevant supplied rule enables a false conclusion
on the intended input domain. Static soundness passes.

## 6. Fresh non-vacuity test

I authored `spec-vacuity-reviewer.k` in scratch. It uses the concrete satisfying
input Mercury/Neptune but falsely requires the empty tuple.

The dry run parsed and built the claim successfully with exit 0
([stage6-vacuity-dry-run.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage6-vacuity-dry-run.log)).

six actual values Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus against the false
empty target
([stage6-vacuity-proof.log](/audit-output/evidence/stage6-vacuity-proof.log)).

This is a reachable, result-bearing failure, distinct from the executed-body
mutation in Stage 4. Non-vacuity passes.

## 7. Proven versus assumed accounting

### What the K proof establishes

Under the supplied semantics and the standard initial configuration, the exact
submitted `bf` body has the following partial-correctness behavior for every
pair of string values:

- if both values are the encodings of valid planet names, the returned tuple is
  exactly the planets strictly between them in the fixed solar order;
- if either value is not a valid name, the returned tuple is empty; and
- execution returns with the initial module environment restored, empty heap
  and stack, `noRet`, `NoExc`, and exit code 0.

The valid part is an exhaustive proof over the contract's finite 8×8 valid
domain. The invalid part is symbolic over arbitrary `IntSeq` string contents.
This is not merely differential testing and not merely the historical
candidate `#Top`; it is the fresh reachability result in Stage 3.
